books.section: Topic 4.9 The Development of an American Culture, B. European Romanticism and American Culture

stimulus.text: Thomas Cole, The Course of Empire: Destruction, 1836, is the fourth of five paintings tracing an imaginary city's rise and fall. A burning classical city fills the canvas: crowds flee across a bridge, a great statue topples from its pedestal at right, and smoke darkens the sky. Cole signed and dated the pedestal "1836."
stimulus.source_note: Painting: Thomas Cole, The Course of Empire: Destruction, 1836 (New-York Historical Society). Public domain; image viewed before writing. Description records only what the painting visibly shows.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Cole's painting most directly warns that which of the following?

options.text: American cities should copy Roman buildings
options.misconception: The city looks Roman, so it is easy to think Cole wanted Americans to copy it.

options.text: The United States had already fallen like Rome
options.misconception: The city is in ruins, so it is easy to think Cole meant America was already ruined.

options.text: Only war can destroy a great nation
options.misconception: Soldiers and flames fill the scene, so it is easy to name war as the only cause.

options.text: Empires collapsing when luxury and pride overtake them

rationales.A: Cole paints Rome burning, not shining; the classical city is a warning, not a model.
rationales.B: The city is imaginary and the series traces a full rise and fall; America is the audience, not the ruin.
rationales.C: The series blames decline on luxury and pride as much as on invaders; war is the end, not the whole cause.
rationales.D: Five paintings carry one city from wilderness to glory to ruin, so the warning is that no empire is safe.
rationales.general:
1. Place this canvas in its series. It is the fourth of five: the city has already risen, and now it falls.
2. Ask what the series is for. A warning that empires, like republics, can fall.
Background from the books: Cole's Course of Empire warned that republics could fall as empires had.
Remember: a series tells its story across all its parts — never judge one canvas alone.

figures.caption: Thomas Cole, The Course of Empire: Destruction, 1836. A burning classical city, crowds fleeing, a statue toppling.
figures.alt: Thomas Cole's 1836 painting of a burning classical city: crowds flee across a bridge while a huge statue topples from its pedestal at right and smoke fills the sky
